canDo: Can follow a 7–8-minute radio interview in the DELF B2 long-listening format (played twice): get the topic and the speakers’ positions on the first listen and fill in details on the second; can recognise uncertain information conveyed by reported speech (il m’a dit que…) and modalisation (il semblerait que, the conditional).
review: Review J12’s reported speech (sequence of tenses) and J19’s modalisation; look back at J28’s nominalised headlines and J27’s formal register (for polite rebuttals in writing and debate).
input: Read: an analysis of radio’s enduring success, an editorial seeking funding for community radio and a listener’s letter protesting the end of a late-night show; listen: an interview with a late-night phone-in host (played twice), a podcast column and a local radio news flash. Strategy: read the questions and predict before the first listen; on the first listen note only keywords and positions; on the second check numbers, examples and reported content.
output: Write: a reply on a media forum to “Is local radio doomed?” (≥250 words), quoting someone else’s view at least once (reported speech) and using two modalising expressions; speak: a 5-minute monologue on “AI-generated voices presenting radio shows”, then a debate on “listener phone-ins: democratic expression or a place to vent?”.
checkpoint: DELF-format self-test: ≥5 of 6 long-listening questions correct after two listens; can recap the interview’s main points from 5 lines of notes; a well-structured 5-minute monologue.
challenge: Today’s challenge: pick an interview or report of 5+ minutes on RFI or TV5MONDE and listen twice, exam-style: first note just 5 keywords, then expand them into 3 reporting sentences (Selon l’invité, … / Il a expliqué que…) and check yourself against the original or the transcript.

questions.why: The article starts from « Pourtant, la radio est toujours là » and analyses why it has lasted (companionship, trust) and how it has adapted (the morning slot, podcasts). A is the opposite of the whole text; C: ad revenue is only mentioned in passing in the third paragraph.
« La radio ne demande ni les yeux ni les mains… Elle accompagne la vie au lieu de l’interrompre ». B isn’t mentioned; C is his colleagues’ mistaken prediction back then.
Reported speech: « ses collègues lui affirmaient que la radio n’aurait bientôt plus qu’un public de retraités » (the conditional = future in the past). A is the opposite; B has no basis.
« La tranche matinale… concentre désormais l’essentiel de l’audience et des recettes publicitaires ». A describes how the rest of the schedule was adjusted; C isn’t mentioned.
s’effacer = to fade, to disappear; tendre à = to tend to. Stations also make podcasts, so the line between the two is increasingly blurred. A and B are distortions.

« Plusieurs observateurs l’attribuent… créerait un sentiment de proximité »: the conditional créerait signals an unproven hypothesis. A doesn’t fit the modalised tone; C: the author doesn’t deny it, only doubts whether it can attract young people.
The editorial stresses their irreplaceable role and calls for action: « Il serait temps de les entendre ». A is the opposite of the text’s praise; B: there is no comparison of audience figures.
« Elles se font l’écho de réalités que les grandes stations nationales ignorent ». Neither A nor C has any basis.
faire les frais de qch = to bear the brunt of something. B and C misread frais literally (as costs).
« une visibilité sur trois ans pour cesser de vivre au jour le jour ». A is rejected by « Ils ne réclament pas des privilèges »; B isn’t mentioned.
« Une démocratie se mesure aussi au nombre de voix qu’elle laisse s’exprimer » raises the local radio question to the level of democracy. Neither A nor C fits.
The title and the whole letter protest against the show being dropped and ask the station to « revenir sur sa décision ». B is the opposite; C isn’t mentioned.
Reported speech: « La direction a expliqué que l’audience nocturne était trop faible ». A and C aren’t mentioned.
« c’est une présence humaine au cœur de la nuit ». A is exactly what she sees as the flaw of the replacement programme; B has no basis.
« ou, si c’est impossible, de maintenir une émission en direct au moins deux nuits par semaine ». A: she clearly says it can’t replace the show; C isn’t mentioned.
The interview covers the late-night phone-in’s listeners, rules and purpose, ending with « ça sert surtout à une chose : tenir compagnie ». B is only part of the audience; C isn’t covered.
Reported speech: « Un auditeur m’a dit un jour que j’étais la seule personne à qui il avait parlé de toute la semaine ». A confuses it with the host’s question; C isn’t mentioned.
« hors antenne, l’équipe lui donne les coordonnées de services d’écoute spécialisés ». A and B aren’t mentioned.
« ce n’est pas un défouloir : chacun peut s’exprimer, à condition de respecter les autres ». A is wrong: an assistant screens the calls; C is exactly what he denies.

« À la radio, on entend une voix, une hésitation, une émotion. Il semblerait que ça désamorce beaucoup de tensions »; il semblerait que expresses a cautious hypothesis. B is how he describes social media; C is wrong: listeners « ne sont pas du tout d’accord ».
« Les auditeurs ont envoyé des centaines de messages, et la station a finalement décidé de la maintenir ». A and B aren’t mentioned.
The column analyses why podcasts are popular and discusses their relationship with radio. A is rejected by « Pas du tout ! »; C isn’t covered.
« D’abord, la liberté… on l’écoute quand on veut, en différé ». B and C aren’t mentioned.
« de bouche à oreille, sans aucune publicité ». A is rejected by « sans aucune publicité »; B isn’t mentioned.
« le podcast a un point faible : il ne connaît pas le direct ». A is something she sees as a strength; C isn’t mentioned.
« pourrait cesser d’émettre »: the conditional of pouvoir expresses possibility, not certainty. A is too definite; C is only background.
aurait décidé and auraient lancé are the news conditional, signalling “unconfirmed”; sous toutes réserves = subject to confirmation. B has no basis; C isn’t why the conditional is used.

V29-01.exZh: In the age of ubiquitous screens, radio is surprisingly resilient.

V29-02.zh: to look like, to be seen as
V29-02.exZh: This old medium looks like a survivor.

V29-03.exZh: The morning slot accounts for most of the audience.

V29-04.exZh: Stations are struggling to keep an increasingly fickle audience loyal.

V29-05.exZh: The rest of the schedule has been completely redesigned.

V29-06.zh: to stand the test of time
V29-06.exZh: Radio has stood the test of time.

V29-07.zh: to shut down, to go out of business
V29-07.exZh: Without funding, several stations could shut down.

V29-08.exZh: Community radio remains an irreplaceable local medium.

V29-09.exZh: These stations give a voice to residents who are never heard elsewhere.

V29-10.exZh: They report on realities that the big stations ignore.

V29-11.exZh: Remote areas would be the first to bear the brunt.

V29-12.exZh: At night, an automated music programme will take over.

V29-13.exZh: Being on air before midnight feels so strange!

V29-14.exZh: He hosts a phone-in between midnight and two in the morning.

V29-15.exZh: My job is to listen attentively to the people who call.

V29-16.zh: to calm things down, to defuse tension
V29-16.exZh: When the tone gets heated, the host tries to calm things down.

V29-17.exZh: An assistant decides who can go on air.

V29-18.zh: a place to let off steam
V29-18.exZh: A phone-in isn’t a place to let off steam.

V29-19.zh: (success, interest) to show no sign of fading
V29-19.exZh: For ten years, the festival’s success has shown no sign of fading.

V29-20.exZh: At night, radio is above all there to keep people company.

V29-21.exZh: You can listen to the show on demand on the metro.

V29-22.exZh: The podcast found its audience by word of mouth.

V29-23.exZh: If the station closes, local news itself is at stake.

V29-24.exZh: The station could stop broadcasting at the end of the year.

V29-25.exZh: The above information is subject to confirmation.
